chapter.title: MemAccess: memory access pattern profiling
chapter.para: To use this tool, you must specify --tool=memaccess on the Valgrind command line.

MemAccess is useful when Memcheck reports many invalid accesses and the individual errors do not make the underlying traversal pattern obvious. It records data loads and stores, attributes them to the guest function containing the accessing instruction, and summarizes how each function walks through memory.

sect1.title: Overview
sect1.para: For every function, MemAccess reports the number of reads and writes, the most common address stride, and one of these access patterns:

listitem.para: At least --sequential-threshold percent of consecutive accesses in that direction advance by exactly the access size, either forwards or backwards.

At least --sequential-threshold percent of consecutive accesses use one constant stride that is not equal to the access size. This includes repeated accesses to one address (stride zero). For example, reading every second element of an array produces a strided pattern.
Neither of the conditions above is met. This includes pointer chasing, hash-table walks, and interleaved traversals that frequently switch between unrelated addresses.
The function has fewer than two accesses in that direction, so no stride can be calculated.

sect1.para: Reads and writes are tracked independently. Read-modify-write operations count as both one read and one write. Instruction fetches are not included. The stride is the difference between consecutive data addresses observed for the same function and direction. Compute the pattern separately for each function so that unrelated functions do not contaminate each other's streams.
Valgrind instruments all guest code, so the table also contains library functions and stack accesses. Focus on the function names from the part of the program being investigated.

sect1.title: Output
sect1.para: A summary table is printed on Valgrind's normal output channel. For example:
sect1.programlisting: Function Reads Writes R-stride R-pattern W-stride W-pattern parse_packet 4096 1024 4 sequential - n/a lookup_chain 731 0 16 strided - n/a
sect1.para: MemAccess also writes folded stack data for flame graph tools. The data is written to memaccess.out.%p by default, where %p is the process ID. Each line has the form:

The counts are memory access counts. Function names are used as frames; this tool intentionally does not unwind the call stack. This makes the data cheap to collect and keeps attribution stable even when debug information for callers is incomplete. Feed the file directly to flamegraph.pl, for example:
Function names have whitespace and semicolons replaced with underscores so that they remain valid folded-stack frame names.

listitem.para: Write folded flame graph data to file. The usual Valgrind file-name substitutions, including %p, are supported.

Set the minimum percentage of transitions that must have a particular stride before a stream is classified as sequential or strided. Lower values classify more streams as regular; higher values require a stronger pattern.

sect1.title: Limitations
sect1.para: MemAccess observes guest virtual addresses. It does not account for physical-page mapping, and Valgrind's own address layout can differ from a native run. The pattern is based on consecutive accesses in program order within one function; it does not reconstruct higher-level objects or loop nesting. Accesses to multiple interleaved buffers in one function share the same stream and may therefore be classified as random. Multi-threaded executions also share one stream per function, so interleaving by different threads can make a regular stream appear random.

The tool is substantially slower than native execution because every load and store calls a helper. Use it after Memcheck has identified the interesting part of a program, or on a reduced reproduction.

As with other Valgrind tools, VEX optimisation can remove guest loads whose results are dead. Such accesses are not observable by MemAccess at the default optimisation level. Use --vex-iropt-level=0 when an exhaustive raw load trace is required.
